Using the engine on your own dataset

Source: vignettes/generic-engine.Rmd
generic-engine.Rmd

groundplotqc checks any set of related tables against a specification you write. This article runs the checks on a small fish survey: three tables of stations, hauls and catches. It reads the survey’s specification, checks its tables as data frames, then as CSV files and from a database, and writes the results to a run folder.

The specification

The specification is the survey’s data dictionary, its code lists, its type map and its missing-value codes, read as the article “Specification files and configuration” reads it.

library(groundplotqc)
example <- function(file) system.file("extdata", "examples", file, package = "groundplotqc")
fish <- gpq_read_spec(
  dictionary = example("fish_dictionary.csv"),
  code_lists = list(
    water_body = example("fish_water_body.csv"), gear = example("fish_gear.csv"),
    species = example("fish_species.csv")
  ),
  column_map = gpq_column_map(
    table = "table", attribute = "field", type = "kind", key_type = "key",
    reference = "parent", lookup = "codes", description = "notes",
    min_value = "low", max_value = "high", min_inclusive = "low_in", max_inclusive = "high_in",
    pattern = "format", max_length = "width", decimals = "places", units = "unit"
  ),
  type_map = gpq_type_map(example("fish_types.csv")),
  sentinels = gpq_sentinels(
    numeric = c(missing = -99, not_applicable = -88),
    character = c(missing = "?", not_applicable = "~"),
    date = c(missing = "?", not_applicable = "~")
  )
)

The tables as data frames

The tables are a named list, one data frame per table of the dictionary. This survey has two mistakes: a catch whose weight is missing, written as NA where the specification’s code for a missing value is -99, and a gear code with a space after it.

tables <- list(
  stations = data.frame(
    station_id = c("S1", "S2"), station_name = c("Long Lake", "Stony River"),
    water_body = c("LK", "RV"), depth = c(1.5, 2.5),
    first_visit = c("2020-06-01", "2020-06-02")
  ),
  hauls = data.frame(
    haul_id = c("H1", "H2", "H3"), station_id = c("S1", "S1", "S2"),
    gear = c("GN", "TN ", "EF"), minutes = c(30L, 45L, 20L),
    haul_date = c("2020-06-01", "2020-06-01", "2020-06-02")
  ),
  catches = data.frame(
    catch_id = c("C1", "C2", "C3", "C4"), haul_id = c("H1", "H1", "H2", "H3"),
    species = c("WAE", "NOP", "YEP", "LKT"), fish_count = c(3L, 1L, 4L, 2L),
    weight = c(1.2, 0.4, NA, 0.9)
  )
)
results <- gpq_check_conformance(tables, fish, group_cols = "water_body", layers = 0:2)

The results summary has one row for each rule, table, column and group. Each issue names its rule, its record and the value that failed. The first table counts the summary’s rows by status; the open issues follow, each with its group column, water_body.

table(results$results$status)
#> 
#>    fail not_run    pass 
#>       2       1     226
open <- results$issues[results$issues$status == "open", ]
open[, c("rule_id", "table_name", "column_name", "record_pk", "value", "water_body")]
#>               rule_id table_name column_name record_pk  value water_body
#>                <char>     <char>      <char>    <char> <char>     <char>
#> 1:             raw_na    catches      weight        C3   <NA>         LK
#> 2: whitespace_padding      hauls        gear        H2    TN          LK

One check doesn’t run: species_unknown_code looks for the survey’s codes for an unknown species, and none are given, so it is recorded as not run, with the reason no_input. The codes are given with the setting unknown_codes (see ?groundplotqc_options).

The tables as CSV files

The same tables can be given as paths of CSV files, here written to a temporary folder. Every column of a CSV file is read as text, as written, so the checks of how a column is stored don’t run on it; they are recorded as not run, with the reason text_input.

folder <- tempfile("fish")
dir.create(folder)
paths <- file.path(folder, paste0(names(tables), ".csv"))
names(paths) <- names(tables)
for (name in names(tables)) {
  data.table::fwrite(tables[[name]], paths[[name]])
}
from_csv <- gpq_check_conformance(paths, fish, group_cols = "water_body", layers = 0:2)
text_input <- from_csv$results$not_run_reason %in% "text_input"
from_csv$results[text_input, c("rule_id", "table_name", "column_name", "not_run_reason")]
#>                      rule_id table_name  column_name not_run_reason
#>                       <char>     <char>       <char>         <char>
#>  1:           class_mismatch   stations   station_id     text_input
#>  2:           class_mismatch   stations station_name     text_input
#>  3:           class_mismatch   stations   water_body     text_input
#>  4:           class_mismatch   stations        depth     text_input
#>  5:           class_mismatch   stations  first_visit     text_input
#>  6:           class_mismatch      hauls      haul_id     text_input
#>  7:           class_mismatch      hauls   station_id     text_input
#>  8:           class_mismatch      hauls         gear     text_input
#>  9:           class_mismatch      hauls      minutes     text_input
#> 10:           class_mismatch      hauls    haul_date     text_input
#> 11:           class_mismatch    catches     catch_id     text_input
#> 12:           class_mismatch    catches      haul_id     text_input
#> 13:           class_mismatch    catches      species     text_input
#> 14:           class_mismatch    catches   fish_count     text_input
#> 15:           class_mismatch    catches       weight     text_input
#> 16: integer_stored_as_double   stations        depth     text_input
#> 17: integer_stored_as_double      hauls      minutes     text_input
#> 18: integer_stored_as_double    catches   fish_count     text_input
#> 19: integer_stored_as_double    catches       weight     text_input

The run’s metadata records each file by its name and SHA-256, with its rows and the separator that was found.

from_csv$metadata$inputs
#>              input         file                                                           sha256                  detail
#>             <char>       <char>                                                           <char>                  <char>
#> 1: tables:stations stations.csv 2624c1e274b91379a059858541673771072af813a7fcab6d15a2a76a56b4b0c4 2 rows; separator comma
#> 2:    tables:hauls    hauls.csv 1e6ddd9a42499a7f0b0f255a076fc44b0d29d59153e1ff7122fe6fa7924cd90e 3 rows; separator comma
#> 3:  tables:catches  catches.csv 23f052b4568fd7dd829c6f71f27cdf7a41566a5fe26a58b01b185b233e511499 4 rows; separator comma

The tables in a database

Tables in a database are read through a DBI connection. Where a table has another name in the database, table_map gives it, such as c(hauls = "survey.hauls") for a table in the schema survey. This part runs where the packages DBI and RSQLite are installed.

connection <- DBI::dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), ":memory:")
DBI::dbWriteTable(connection, "stations", tables$stations)
DBI::dbWriteTable(connection, "fish_hauls", tables$hauls)
DBI::dbWriteTable(connection, "fish_catches", tables$catches)
from_db <- gpq_check_conformance(
  connection, fish,
  table_map = c(hauls = "fish_hauls", catches = "fish_catches"),
  group_cols = "water_body", layers = 0:2
)
from_db$metadata$inputs
#>              input                       file sha256                                              detail
#>             <char>                     <char> <char>                                              <char>
#> 1: tables:stations DBI connection, not hashed   <NA>     2 rows; table stations; driver SQLiteConnection
#> 2:    tables:hauls DBI connection, not hashed   <NA>   3 rows; table fish_hauls; driver SQLiteConnection
#> 3:  tables:catches DBI connection, not hashed   <NA> 4 rows; table fish_catches; driver SQLiteConnection
DBI::dbDisconnect(connection)

The database’s tables give the same results as the data frames, and the metadata names each table as the database names it, with the driver’s class.

The run folder

gpq_write_results() writes a run’s results to a folder named by its run ID, and gpq_read_results() reads them back.

output <- tempfile("runs")
gpq_write_results(results, output)
run_dir <- file.path(output, results$metadata$run$run_id)
list.files(run_dir, recursive = TRUE)
#>  [1] "metadata/clashes.csv"       "metadata/inputs.csv"       
#>  [3] "metadata/preflight.csv"     "metadata/rules.csv"        
#>  [5] "metadata/run.csv"           "metadata/self_test.csv"    
#>  [7] "metadata/settings.csv"      "metadata/spec_manifest.csv"
#>  [9] "tables/corrections.csv"     "tables/issues.csv"         
#> [11] "tables/results.csv"
again <- gpq_read_results(run_dir)
identical(again$issues, results$issues)
#> [1] TRUE

Issue classes

Each issue has a class: source, for the provider to fix in their data; harmonization, made when the data was converted to the specification’s form; or unclassified. gpq_classify_issues() gives each issue its rule’s class, unless one of your overrides gives it another. Where a rule’s class is depends, the evidence you give can settle it, and class_basis says what decided each issue’s class.

Two more mistakes give the survey such issues: a station 600 metres deep, past the dictionary’s 500, and a haul of 900 minutes, past its 600. Both are value_above_max, a rule whose class is depends.

planted <- tables
planted$stations$depth[2] <- 600
planted$hauls$minutes[3] <- 900L
checked <- gpq_check_conformance(planted, fish, group_cols = "water_body", layers = 0:3)

An override records your decision: the long haul is the provider’s to fix. A computed row says the pipeline computes the stations’ depth, so a wrong depth is harmonization. Its column water_body is the run’s group column, and "*" stands for every value.

overrides <- data.frame(
  fingerprint = NA, rule_id = "value_above_max", table_name = "hauls",
  column_name = "minutes", issue_class = "source", who = "A. Reviewer",
  when = "2026-10-22", why = "The gear log gives 20 minutes."
)
computed <- data.frame(
  table_name = "stations", column_name = "depth", water_body = "*", derivation = "formula"
)
gpq_classify_issues(
  checked$issues,
  rules = NULL, evidence = list(computed = computed), overrides = overrides
)
checked$issues[, c(
  "rule_id", "table_name", "column_name", "value", "status", "issue_class", "class_basis"
)]
#>               rule_id table_name column_name  value        status   issue_class class_basis
#>                <char>     <char>      <char> <char>        <char>        <char>      <char>
#> 1:             raw_na    catches      weight   <NA>          open harmonization     default
#> 2: whitespace_padding      hauls        gear    TN           open harmonization     default
#> 3:   code_not_in_list      hauls        gear    TN  not_evaluated  unclassified     default
#> 4:    value_below_min    catches      weight   <NA> not_evaluated  unclassified     default
#> 5:    value_above_max   stations       depth    600          open harmonization    computed
#> 6:    value_above_max      hauls     minutes    900          open        source    override
#> 7:    value_above_max    catches      weight   <NA> not_evaluated  unclassified     default
#> 8:  decimals_exceeded    catches      weight   <NA> not_evaluated  unclassified     default

The other issues keep their rules’ classes, with class_basis default. An issue whose rule’s class is depends and that nothing settles is unclassified; the setting fallback_class gives such a rule a class of its own (see ?groundplotqc_options).

Reports

gpq_build_reports() builds one report and one issues CSV for each report unit, here each water body. It writes them into the run’s folder, so the run is written first, with gpq_write_results().

output <- tempfile("runs")
gpq_write_results(checked, output)
files <- gpq_build_reports(checked, output)
basename(files)
#> [1] "LK.html"       "LK_issues.csv" "RV.html"       "RV_issues.csv"

Each unit’s issues CSV lists every issue of its report, one per row. Here are six of its columns for the first water body.

csv <- data.table::fread(files[[2L]], encoding = "UTF-8")
csv[, c("water_body", "table_name", "column_name", "rule_id", "issue_class", "value")]
#>    water_body table_name column_name            rule_id   issue_class  value
#>        <char>     <char>      <char>             <char>        <char> <char>
#> 1:         LK      hauls        gear   code_not_in_list  unclassified     TN
#> 2:         LK    catches      weight             raw_na harmonization       
#> 3:         LK    catches      weight    value_above_max  unclassified       
#> 4:         LK    catches      weight    value_below_min  unclassified       
#> 5:         LK    catches      weight  decimals_exceeded  unclassified       
#> 6:         LK      hauls        gear whitespace_padding harmonization     TN

To read a unit’s report, open its reports/<unit>.html in the run’s folder in a browser. Each report is one file that needs no internet connection.
